opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting eval for a few reasons. One is that a lot of the benchmarks we've relied on are getting saturated. Models are doing extremely well on math competitions and coding challenges, and it's getting harder to tell how much better one model is than another. You want evaluations that are open-ended, where there isn't a ceiling and you can keep measuring progress.

Poker bots fit that well. It's not "here's a problem, get the right answer." It's "build something that performs well against other agents," and there's no known perfect answer. You can always build a stronger bot, and you can pit bots against each other, so you get a natural ranking that keeps scaling as models improve.

It also tests a lot of things at once. The model has to understand game theory and imperfect-information reasoning: bluffing, balancing your range, not being exploitable. Then it has to turn that into working code, manage a fairly long engineering task, and debug and iterate. That's much closer to real-world work than a single question with a single answer.

And having spent years building poker AIs myself, I find it fun to see what models come up with. I know how hard it is to do well. Doing it from scratch requires real research taste: knowing which approaches are promising, which abstractions to use, and how to allocate a limited compute budget. Those are exactly the skills we want these models to develop if they're going to help with research. So it's a nice proxy for whether a model can do something research-like end to end, not just answer trivia or solve a well-specified puzzle.

r001.rationale: The response says building a bot from scratch tests game-theoretic reasoning and research skills, but it does not mention scarce open-source poker-bot code as the reason this tests the model’s own reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the reason it's interesting is that poker is kind of a uniquely hard problem to solve, and it's a problem where the answer isn't just sitting in the training data. If you ask a model to write a chess engine, there's a huge amount of existing code and existing knowledge about how to do that well. With poker, especially if you're talking about full no-limit Texas hold'em, the techniques that actually work, things like counterfactual regret minimization, real-time search with imperfect information, abstraction, those are things that took the research community a long time to figure out. And even if you know the techniques, actually implementing them correctly and making them scale is genuinely difficult. There are a lot of ways to get it subtly wrong.

So what I like about it as an evaluation is that it's end-to-end. It's not a single question with a single answer. The model has to understand the game, understand the theory, make engineering decisions, debug its own code, and then you can just test the result. You can play the bot against a known strong baseline and see how it does. It's very hard to fake that. You can't memorize your way to a bot that wins.

The other thing I'd say is that it tests reasoning under imperfect information, which I think is much closer to what matters in the real world than something like chess or Go. In the real world you almost never have full visibility into what the other party knows or wants. So a model that can reason well about hidden information and about how to build systems that reason about hidden information, that's a meaningful signal about how useful it's going to be on problems that actually matter.

And honestly, part of it is personal. I spent years of my life building these systems, so I have a very good sense of what "good" looks like and where the hard parts are. That makes it a nice yardstick for me to judge how far these models have come.

r001.rationale: The response says poker solutions are not readily available in training data and that bots test reasoning, but it does not explain that open-source poker-bot code is scarce.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful because it’s an open-ended task where you can actually measure how well the result works. You’re not just asking the model a question about poker and judging whether its answer sounds reasonable. You’re asking it to build something, and then you can play that bot against other bots and see how it performs.

And poker forces you to deal with uncertainty. You don’t know the other player’s cards, and the right strategy depends on what they might have and how they might play. A bot can know all the rules and still be terrible at the game. So there’s a meaningful gap between producing code that runs and producing a strong strategy.

What’s especially interesting to me is whether the model can close that gap through experimentation. Can it test its bot, identify weaknesses, and improve it? That gives you a way to evaluate the whole process of solving a problem, rather than just the first answer the model gives.

sol-6.1.text:
Poker is a useful test because it’s a game of imperfect information. You don’t get to see your opponent’s cards, so you have to reason about what they might have, what they believe you have, and how your actions affect those beliefs. Just calculating the strongest hand isn’t enough.

And asking a model to build a poker bot tests something broader than whether it can answer a poker question. Can it turn its understanding into code, test that code, find mistakes, and improve the strategy? You can then have the bots actually play and measure how well they do. That gives you a concrete way to distinguish a model that can explain a convincing strategy from one that can build something that works.

r001.rationale: The response says building and testing a poker bot assesses reasoning and coding, but it does not mention scarce open-source poker-bot code as the reason this tests the model’s own reasoning.
